claims.claim: B. bronchiseptica contributes to exacerbate respiratory symptoms in co-infections with other respiratory pathogens, including the development of acute pulmonary disease and bronchopneumonia.
claims.source: In co-infections with other respiratory pathogens B. bronchiseptica contributes to exacerbate respiratory symptoms, including the development of acute pulmonary disease and bronchopneumonia, and ultimately host death (Brockmeier et al., 2008; Loving et al., 2010; Schulz et al., 2014; Kureljušić et al., 2016; Hughes et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Parasitic helminths commonly stimulate a Th2 anti-inflammatory immune response that interferes with the Th1 response developed against B. bronchiseptica.
claims.source: Parasitic helminths commonly stimulate a Th2 anti-inflammatory immune response that interferes with the Th1 response developed against B. bronchiseptica and related species (Brady et al., 1999; Pathak et al., 2012; Thakar et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous immunological studies.

claims.claim: Rabbits co-infected with either T. retortaeformis or G. strigosum carried higher B. bronchiseptica infections in the nasal cavity but there were no significant differences in the size and duration of infection in the lungs, when compared to rabbits infected with bacteria alone.
claims.source: We recently showed that rabbits co-infected with either T. retortaeformis or G. strigosum carried higher B. bronchiseptica infections in the nasal cavity but there were no significant differences in the size and duration of infection in the lungs, when compared to rabbits infected with bacteria alone (Pathak et al., 2010; Pathak et al., 2012; Thakar et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous experimental work by the authors.

claims.claim: T. retortaeformis is reduced or cleared from the small intestine while G. strigosum persists with high intensities in the stomach.
claims.source: These two helminths stimulate a similar immune response, however, while the former is reduced or cleared from the small intestine, the latter persists with high intensities in the stomach (Cattadori et al., 2005; Cattadori et al., 2008; Cattadori et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claims.claim: Neutrophils and antibodies IgA and IgG are important to bacterial clearance from the lungs.
claims.source: The modeling of the immune network in B. bronchiseptica-T. retortaeformis rabbits and B. bronchiseptica alone animals suggested that neutrophils and antibodies IgA and IgG are important to bacterial clearance from the lungs (Thakar et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous modeling work cited.

claims.claim: There was large variation in the level at which B. bronchiseptica was shed both within and between the four types of infection.
claims.source: There was large variation in the level at which B. bronchiseptica was shed both within and between the four types of infection (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data and shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: 3 out of 16 B. bronchiseptica only animals did not shed at all.
claims.source: Some rabbits consistently shed large amounts of CFUs while others were low shedders or did not shed at all, specifically: 3 out of 16 for B. bronchiseptica only animals (B), 1 out of 23 for B. bronchiseptica-G. strigosum (BG), 3 out of 20 for B. bronchiseptica-T. retortaeformis (BT) and 0 out of 24 for the triple infection (BTG).
claims.evidence: This is a direct count from experimental observations.

claims.claim: High shedders were found during the first 60 days post infection.
claims.source: High shedders were found during the first 60 days post infection, although some of these rabbits continued to shed a large number of bacteria well beyond this time (Figures 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claims.claim: The level of shedding was significantly higher in rabbits co-infected with helminths than B. bronchiseptica only animals (BTG: 0.42, 0.31–0.54; BG: 0.32, 0.25–0.41; BT: 0.26, 0.18–0.35 and B: 0.02,–0.01-0.03; p<0.05).
claims.source: The level of shedding was significantly higher in rabbits co-infected with helminths than B. bronchiseptica only animals (mean shedding (CFU/s) and 95% CI, BTG: 0.42, 0.31–0.54; BG: 0.32, 0.25–0.41; BT: 0.26, 0.18–0.35 and B: 0.02,–0.01-0.03; Kruskal-Wallis test with Bonferroni correction for multiple testing, for all: p<0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: No significant differences in shedding were observed among the three co-infected groups.
claims.source: When we considered the co-infected hosts, no significant differences were observed among the three groups (p>0.05) although the triple infection showed a tendency for higher shedding (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Up to 55% of the shedding events were classified as null, where rabbits interacted with the petri dish but did not shed even though they were known to be infected.
claims.source: Across the four infections up to 55% of the shedding events were classified as null, where rabbits interacted with the petri dish but did not shed even though they were known to be infected (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The highest percentage of null shedding was found in the B. bronchiseptica only group (56.2%).
claims.source: The highest percentage was found in the B. bronchiseptica only group (56.2%), followed by the dual infections (BT: 40.3% and BG: 29.8%) and last the triple infection BTG (25.8%) (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a direct calculation from experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The BTG group showed the largest variation in the level of shedding (Negative Binomial k=0.21, 0.16–0.26).
claims.source: This latter group showed the largest variation in the level of shedding (Negative Binomial k and 95% CI, BTG: 0.21, 0.16–0.26) followed by the dual infections BG (0.37, 0.29–0.45) and BT (0.45, 0.33–0.57); for all, the distribution was not significantly different from the frequency data (p>0.05).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical modeling of the experimental data.

claims.claim: The presence of helminths increased the level of bacteria shed in the environment and the frequency of these events.
claims.source: These findings suggest that the presence of helminths increased the level of bacteria shed in the environment and the frequency of these events.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Having helminths increased the variation in the magnitude of shedding events among rabbits within the same group as well as between groups.
claims.source: Having helminths also increased the variation in the magnitude of these events among rabbits within the same group as well as between groups.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Co-infections with helminths should lead to a higher probability of B. bronchiseptica onward transmission given a contact.
claims.source: Together these findings indicate that co-infections with helminths, irrespective of the species, should lead to a higher probability of B. bronchiseptica onward transmission given a contact.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in shedding levels.

claims.claim: Using the 99th percentile threshold of CFU/s=0.27 from B. bronchiseptica only rabbits, none of the B rabbits can be classified as supershedders.
claims.source: If we estimate this threshold using B. bronchiseptica only infected animals, and define supershedders as the hosts that have at least one shedding event above this threshold, for example the 99th percentile, our cut-off value is CFU/s=0.27 (Figure 3). This indicates that none of the rabbits with B. bronchiseptica (0 out of 13) can be classified as supershedders.
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Using the 99th percentile threshold from B only rabbits, 59% of BG, 53% of BT, and 42% of BTG rabbits are supershedders.
claims.source: However, if we apply the same cut-off to the co-infected groups the percentage is considerably high, namely: 59% (13 out of 22) for BG, 53% (9 out of 17) for BT and 42% (10 out of 24) for the BTG group.
claims.evidence: This is based on applying the threshold to experimental data.

claims.claim: Using the 99th percentile threshold from the whole dataset (CFU/s=8.58), 0% of B, 32% of BG, 18% of BT, and 21% of BTG rabbits had at least one supershedding event.
claims.source: When we apply this approach the 99th percentile threshold is now CFU/s=8.58 and the fraction of hosts with, at least, one supershedding event above this value is: 0% (0 out of 13) for B, 32% (7 out of 22) for BG, 18% (3 out of 17) BT and 21% (5 out of 24) for BTG (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the entire experimental dataset.

claims.claim: Using the 95th percentile threshold from the whole dataset (CFU/s=2.71), the number of rabbits with at least one supershedding event is 0% for B, 45% for BG, 29% for BT, and 29% for BTG.
claims.source: Similarly, if we select the less limiting 95th percentile threshold, the new common value decreases to CFU/s=2.71 and the number of rabbits with at least one supershedding event is still zero for B but increases to 45% (10 out of 22) for BG, 29% (5 out of 17) for BT and 29% (7 out of 24) for BTG (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the entire experimental dataset.

claims.claim: Supershedding events were found more often in the initial four/five weeks post infection.
claims.source: Consistent with the general pattern of shedding, supershedding events were found more often in the initial four/five weeks post infection (Figures 1 and 2), although later events were also observed, especially for the BG and BTG groups, and with some rabbits contributing multiple times.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claims.claim: There was a rapid bacterial replication following the initial inoculum.
claims.source: Consistently among the four types of infection, simulations indicated that there was a rapid bacterial replication following the initial inoculum, the growth rate, r, was high for BTG (group level value and [95% CI]: 1.47 [1.10–1.83]) and BG (1.18 [0.83–1.54]), less so for BT (1.01 [0.83–1.18]) and much lower for B single infection (0.06 [0.006–0.12]) (Tables 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on model simulations fitted to experimental data.

claims.claim: Model fitting well captured the empirical trends of neutrophils and specific antibodies over time.
claims.source: Model fitting well captured the empirical trends of neutrophils and specific antibodies over time, both as a profile representative of each type of infection and as a trend of every rabbit within each group (Table 2, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of model performance against experimental data.

claims.claim: In all four groups, neutrophils showed the fastest rate of increase, followed by specific IgA and then specific IgG.
claims.source: In all four groups, neutrophils showed the fastest rate of increase, a1, with a tendency to be faster in B. bronchiseptica only rabbits, followed by specific IgA and then specific IgG (Table 2, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is based on model parameter estimates from experimental data.

claims.claim: Neutrophils were the fastest to decrease and to return to original values with the neutralization of bacteria from the respiratory tract.
claims.source: Neutrophils were also the fastest to decrease, at a rate b1, and to return to original values with the neutralization, albeit no complete clearance, of bacteria from the respiratory tract (Figures 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: This is based on model simulations and experimental observations.

claims.claim: B. bronchiseptica is removed from lungs and trachea but persists in the nasal cavity.
claims.source: As reported in our previous studies of this system, B. bronchiseptica is removed from lungs and trachea but persists in the nasal cavity (Pathak et al., 2010; Pathak et al., 2012; Thakar et al., 2012), a pattern also observed in mice (Kirimanjeswara et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claims.claim: IgG reached the asymptotic value at around 20 days post infection and remained high throughout the trials.
claims.source: The increase of specific IgA and IgG was slow, however, once IgG reached the asymptotic value at around 20 days post infection, it remained high throughout the trials, while IgA peaked around day 20 and slowly decreased thereafter, although it had not fallen to baseline levels by the end of the trials (Figures 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the experimental data and model simulations shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claims.claim: The relative contribution of neutrophils, IgA, and IgG to B. bronchiseptica neutralization varied among the four types of infection.
claims.source: The relative contribution of the three immune variables to B. bronchiseptica neutralization, c1, c2, c3, varied among the four types of infection.
claims.evidence: This is based on model parameter estimates from experimental data.

claims.claim: Neutrophils primarily controlled bacteria in the single infection.
claims.source: Model fittings suggested that neutrophils primarily controlled bacteria in the single infection, whereas a combination of neutrophils and specific IgG were probably important in BTG rabbits (Table 2, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is based on model parameter estimates and simulations.

claims.claim: A combination of neutrophils and specific IgG were probably important in BTG rabbits.
claims.source: Model fittings suggested that neutrophils primarily controlled bacteria in the single infection, whereas a combination of neutrophils and specific IgG were probably important in BTG rabbits (Table 2, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is based on model parameter estimates and simulations.

claims.claim: The coupling of IgG and IgA could contribute to explain the neutralization of bacteria in the BT group.
claims.source: The coupling of IgG and IgA could contribute to explain the neutralization of bacteria in the BT group while neutrophils and IgG appeared to be relevant in the BG group.
claims.evidence: This is based on model parameter estimates and simulations.

claims.claim: Neutrophils and IgG appeared to be relevant in the BG group.
claims.source: The coupling of IgG and IgA could contribute to explain the neutralization of bacteria in the BT group while neutrophils and IgG appeared to be relevant in the BG group.
claims.evidence: This is based on model parameter estimates and simulations.

claims.claim: Neutrophils are expected to primarily control B. bronchiseptica early on in the infection.
claims.source: Given the early reaction of neutrophils, they are expected to primarily control B. bronchiseptica early on in the infection, while specific IgG and, secondly, specific IgA appear to be more important at a later time, as they decreased more slowly, such is the case for IgA, or remained consistently high over the course of the infection, like for IgG (Figures 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal dynamics observed in the data and model.

claims.claim: Specific IgG and IgA appear to be more important at a later time in controlling B. bronchiseptica.
claims.source: Given the early reaction of neutrophils, they are expected to primarily control B. bronchiseptica early on in the infection, while specific IgG and, secondly, specific IgA appear to be more important at a later time, as they decreased more slowly, such is the case for IgA, or remained consistently high over the course of the infection, like for IgG (Figures 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal dynamics observed in the data and model.

claims.claim: The immune response changed both between individuals within a group and between groups.
claims.source: An investigation of the posterior parameter estimations confirmed that the immune response changed both between individuals within a group and between groups (Appendix 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of model parameter estimates.

claims.claim: The estimated time to reach the peak of shedding was between 10 and 12 days post infection for the co-infected groups.
claims.source: The estimated time to reach the peak of shedding was between 10 and 12 days post infection for the co-infected groups, specifically: 9 days for BTG, 11 days for BT and 12 days for BG.
claims.evidence: This is based on model simulations fitted to experimental data.

claims.claim: The peak value of shedding was 14,185 CFU/day (11.06–12,258,022) for BTG, 8,266 (5.89–10,119,754) for BG, and 7,863 (29.57–2,213,310) for BT.
claims.source: For example, the peak value (CFU/day; 95% CIs) was: 14,185 (11.06–12,258,022) for BTG, 8,266 (5.89–10,119,754) for BG and 7,863 (29.57–2,213,310) for BT.
claims.evidence: This is based on model simulations fitted to experimental data.

claims.claim: Rabbits from the BTG infection exhibited the most rapid increase of shedding, the highest levels and the slowest decline post-peak.
claims.source: Rabbits from the BTG infection exhibited the most rapid increase of shedding, the highest levels and the slowest decline post-peak, suggesting a possible synergistic effect of the two helminths.
claims.evidence: This is based on model simulations and experimental observations.

claims.claim: The two helminths in the BTG infection may have a synergistic effect.
claims.source: Rabbits from the BTG infection exhibited the most rapid increase of shedding, the highest levels and the slowest decline post-peak, suggesting a possible synergistic effect of the two helminths.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on observed patterns.

claims.claim: The BT group showed the most rapid decline in shedding.
claims.source: The BT group showed the most rapid decline, while rabbits from the BG group maintained a trend intermediate between the BTG and BT groups (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is based on model simulations and experimental observations shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Rabbits showed rapid changes in the level of shedding between consecutive samplings, where bursts of bacteria alternated to low or no shedding in a matter of a few days.
claims.source: Rabbits showed rapid changes in the level of shedding between consecutive samplings, where bursts of bacteria alternated to low or no shedding in a matter of a few days.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from experimental data.

claims.claim: This rapid dynamic could not be explained by the intensity of infection and related immune responses at the scale used to record such data.
claims.source: This rapid dynamic could not be explained by the intensity of infection and related immune responses at the scale used to record such data.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of model limitations based on comparison with data.

claims.claim: Changes in local conditions, such as variation in the severity of tissue inflammation or control of bacteria at the mucosa level, had a stronger impact on fast changes in shedding.
claims.source: Instead, it is possible that changes in local conditions, such as variation in the severity of tissue inflammation or control of bacteria at the mucosa level, including changes in the amount of mucus formation and expulsion, had a stronger impact on these fast changes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for patterns not captured by the model.

claims.claim: Co-infected rabbits sniffled more frequently than B. bronchiseptica only animals.
claims.source: We also noted that co-infected rabbits sniffled more frequently than B. bronchiseptica only animals (Pathak's pers. obs.) and, probably, further contributed to alter the frequency and intensity of these events.
claims.evidence: This is based on personal observation during experiments.

claims.claim: An increase in the rate of bacterial neutralization led to a proportional decrease of the peak of shedding and the time to reach this peak.
claims.source: Findings showed that an increase in the rate of bacterial neutralization, μc , and, secondly, in the mmune growth rate, μa, led to a proportional decrease of the peak of shedding and, to a lesser extent, the time to reach this peak (Appendix 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on sensitivity analysis of the model.

claims.claim: The strongest negative impact on shedding was caused by changes in neutrophil and IgG rates.
claims.source: Among the three immune variables, the strongest negative impact on shedding was caused by changes in neutrophil (c1 or a1) and IgG (c3 or a3) rates.
claims.evidence: This is based on sensitivity analysis of the model.

claims.claim: An increase in bacterial growth rate was associated with a higher peak of shedding and a shorter time to reach this peak.
claims.source: As expected, an increase in bacterial growth rate, r, was associated with a higher peak of shedding and, consequently, a shorter time to reach this peak (Appendix 1—figures 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on sensitivity analysis of the model.

claims.claim: The three co-infections exhibited comparable trends and were more sensitive to immune changes than B. bronchiseptica only infected rabbits.
claims.source: Overall, the three co-infections exhibited comparable trends and were more sensitive to immune changes than B. bronchiseptica only infected rabbits.
claims.evidence: This is based on sensitivity analysis of the model.

claims.claim: The weak response of the B group was probably caused by the very low bacterial growth rate (r=0.06) and thus shedding, suggesting a stronger immune control.
claims.source: The weak response of the latter group was probably caused by the very low bacterial growth rate (r=0.06) and thus shedding, suggesting a stronger immune control.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on model parameter estimates.

claims.claim: Gastrointestinal helminths can impact the severity and time course of respiratory bacterial infections.
claims.source: There is increasing evidence that gastrointestinal helminths can impact the severity and time course of respiratory bacterial infections (Brady et al., 1999; Lass et al., 2013; Diniz et al., 2010; Ezenwa et al., 2010; Babu and Nutman, 2016; Long et al., 2019); however, how they affect the dynamics of shedding remains to be determined.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The two helminths significantly increased the level, the variation and the duration of shedding, along with enhancing the frequency of supershedding events.
claims.source: Empirical findings showed that the two helminths, taken as a single species or as a pair, significantly increased the level, the variation and the duration of shedding, along with enhancing the frequency of supershedding events.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claims.claim: These changes in shedding were related to the significant growth of bacteria in the respiratory tract.
claims.source: Model estimates suggested that these changes were related to the significant growth of bacteria in the respiratory tract.
claims.evidence: This is based on model simulations.

claims.claim: The development of an immune response controlled the infection and led to the waning but not the complete clearance of B. bronchiseptica.
claims.source: The developed of an immune response controlled the infection and led to the waning but not the complete clearance of B. bronchiseptica.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations and model simulations.

claims.claim: The decline of shedding in the first 90 days post infection could be explained by the immune-mediated clearance of B. bronchiseptica from the lungs.
claims.source: The decline of shedding in the first 90 days post infection could be explained by the immune-mediated clearance of B. bronchiseptica from the lungs, previously reported using data from these experiments (Pathak et al., 2010; Pathak et al., 2012; Thakar et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on model simulations and previous experimental findings.

claims.claim: The reduced but ongoing shedding later in the experiments could be the result of the weak control of bacteria in the nasal cavity.
claims.source: In contrast, the reduced but ongoing shedding later in the experiments could be the result of the weak control of bacteria in the nasal cavity (Pathak et al., 2010; Pathak et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on model simulations and previous experimental findings.

claims.claim: The two helminth species appeared not to change the general trend of immune variables but the timing and intensity of their relative contribution.
claims.source: We found that neutrophils quickly increased and contributed to bacteria neutralization early on, these were then followed by antibodies that developed more slowly and with an initial delay in the co-infected hosts. The two helminth species appeared not to change the general trend of these variables but the timing and intensity of their relative contribution and, with this, temporal changes in the level of shedding.
claims.evidence: This is based on model simulations and experimental observations.

claims.claim: Both T. retortaeformis and G. strigosum elicit a Th-2 immune response.
claims.source: We previously showed that both helminths elicit a Th-2 immune response (Murphy et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2013; Cattadori et al., 2019), however, while T. retortaeformis was cleared, or significantly reduced from the small intestine, G. strigosum persisted with high intensities in the stomach (Cattadori et al., 2005; Cattadori et al., 2008; Cattadori et al., 2019; Murphy et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2013; Mignatti et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claims.claim: The faster decline of shedding in BT rabbits could have been caused by the stronger immune control of B. bronchiseptica, probably facilitated by the rapid clearance of T. retortaeformis.
claims.source: It is conceivable to think that the faster decline of shedding in rabbits from the BT than the BG or BTG group could have been caused by the stronger immune control of B. bronchiseptica, probably facilitated by the rapid clearance of T. retortaeformis (Thakar et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on observed patterns and previous findings.

claims.claim: The persistence of G. strigosum in the stomach probably contributed to delay the decline of shedding and to increase the magnitude of these events.
claims.source: In contrast, the persistence of G. strigosum in the stomach probably contributed to delay the decline of shedding and to increase the magnitude of these events, including increasing the frequency of supershedding.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on observed patterns.

claims.claim: In the BTG triple infection the two helminths appeared to have a positive synergistic effect particularly in delaying the decline of shedding.
claims.source: Interestingly, in the BTG triple infection the two helminths appeared to have a positive synergistic effect particularly in delaying the decline of shedding.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on observed patterns in the data.

claims.claim: T. retortaeformis and G. strigosum are commonly found in populations of rabbits.
claims.source: Given these patterns, and considering that T. retortaeformis and G. strigosum are commonly found in populations of rabbits, it is not surprising if these helminths play an important role to the rapid transmission and persistence of B. bronchiseptica in natural settings.
claims.evidence: This is based on knowledge of natural rabbit populations.

claims.claim: The annual prevalence of B. bronchiseptica in a free-living population of rabbits ranged between 88% and 97%.
claims.source: For example, the serological study of a free-living population of rabbits showed that the annual prevalence of B. bronchiseptica ranged between 88% and 97% (Pathak et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous field study.

claims.claim: 65% of rabbits in a free-living population were co-infected with B. bronchiseptica and G. strigosum.
claims.source: Of these rabbits 65% were co-infected with B. bronchiseptica and G. strigosum, and both bacterial prevalence and helminth intensity increased with rabbit age.
claims.evidence: This is based on data from a previous field study.

claims.claim: About 60% of adult rabbits in a free-living population carried BTG infections.
claims.source: Although the study did not examine these patterns in dual or triple infections with T. retortaeformis, about 60% of adult rabbits were found to carry BTG infections (unpubl. data), suggesting that rabbits co-infected with helminths represent a large fraction of this host population and, together with the dual infections, are probably responsible for the high prevalence of B. bronchiseptica throughout the years.
claims.evidence: This is based on unpublished data from field observations.

claims.claim: The combined effect of antigen-antibody complex and phagocytosis, activated by neutrophils, were important for bacterial removal from the lungs.
claims.source: Recent Boolean modeling of the whole immune network to B. bronchiseptica infection indicated that the combined effect of antigen-antibody complex and phagocytosis, activated by neutrophils among others, were important for bacterial removal from the lungs (Thakar et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous modeling work.

claims.claim: Serum antibodies cleared B. bronchiseptica from lungs and trachea of wild-type and B-cell-deficient mice within 3 days post inoculation.
claims.source: The important role of antibodies to B. bronchiseptica control was empirically highlighted in the mouse model where serum antibodies (which include IgG isotypes and IgA) cleared B. bronchiseptica from lungs and trachea of wild-type and B-cell-deficient mice within 3 days post inoculation (Kirimanjeswara et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claims.claim: IgA was found to be necessary for the reduction of bacterial numbers in the nasal cavity of mice.
claims.source: Similarly, IgA was found to be necessary for the reduction of bacterial numbers in the nasal cavity of mice (Wolfe et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claims.claim: There was an early peak of neutrophils in the blood of rabbits infected with the two helminths, likely a consequence of gut bacteria infiltrating in the mucosa damaged during helminth establishment.
claims.source: In our previous work we found an early peak of neutrophils in the blood of rabbits infected with our two helminths and suggested that this was likely a consequence of gut bacteria infiltrating in the mucosa damaged during helminth establishment in the gastrointestinal tract (Murphy et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous experimental observations and interpretation.

claims.claim: Previous work found no temporal differences in bacterial clearance from the lungs of rabbits from the B and the BT groups.
claims.source: Although we were not able to disentangle the proportion of neutrophils that were stimulated by and directed against B. bronchiseptica, previous work by Thakar et al., 2012 found no temporal differences in bacterial clearance from the lungs of rabbits from the B and the BT groups, suggesting that there is probably no significant interference from the gut-stimulated neutrophils.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claims.claim: Gut-restricted helminths could enhance the neutrophil response in the respiratory tract in mice co-infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Heligmosomoides polygyrus.
claims.source: The evidence that gut-restricted helminths could enhance the neutrophil response in the respiratory tract was showed in mice co-infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the lungs and Heligmosomoides polygyrus in the gastrointestinal tract (Long et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claims.claim: Survival rate was improved in mice co-infected with P. aeruginosa and H. polygyrus compared to mice with bacteria alone.
claims.source: This study found a higher recruitment of neutrophils in the lungs together with an increase of CD4 +T cells and Th2 cytokine expression. Interestingly, survival rate was improved in co-infected mice than mice with bacteria alone, suggesting that neutrophils, rather than a Th2 response, dominated in the lungs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claims.claim: TLR4-mutant mice infected with B. bronchiseptica poorly controlled bacterial growth and shedding.
claims.source: Work by Rolin et al., 2014 showed that TLR4-mutant mice infected with B. bronchiseptica poorly controlled bacterial growth and shedding.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claims.claim: In TLR4-mutant mice, the depletion of neutrophils did not affect the level of infection but decreased individual shedding.
claims.source: Animals exhibited heavy neutrophil infiltration in the lungs, however, the depletion of neutrophils did not affect the level of infection but decreased individual shedding.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

results.result: Helminth co-infection significantly increases B. bronchiseptica shedding levels, variation, and frequency compared to bacterial infection alone. Co-infected rabbits (BTG, BG, BT) shed significantly more bacteria than B-only animals (p<0.05), with mean shedding ranging from 0.26-0.42 CFU/s for co-infected groups versus 0.02 CFU/s for B-only. Co-infection also increased variation in shedding magnitude both within and between groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C26, C27, C31, C32, and C68 collectively provide strong experimental evidence with appropriate statistical testing (Kruskal-Wallis with Bonferroni correction) showing significantly higher shedding in helminth co-infected rabbits. The data include quantitative measurements with confidence intervals and p-values, supported by visual evidence in Figures 1-3.

results.result: Helminth co-infection promotes supershedding events in rabbits. Using the 99th percentile threshold from the whole dataset (CFU/s=8.58), 0% of B-only rabbits but 18-32% of co-infected rabbits generated at least one supershedding event. The choice of threshold definition significantly affects supershedding classification, with thresholds based on single infections overestimating supershedding in co-infected hosts.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37, C99, and C100 provide quantitative analysis of supershedding using multiple threshold definitions (95th and 99th percentiles). The statistical approach is sound, demonstrating that threshold selection matters and that co-infected rabbits show substantially higher rates of supershedding regardless of threshold choice. The analysis is supported by Figure 3.

results.result: A mathematical model incorporating neutrophils, IgA, and IgG explains differences in shedding dynamics between infection groups through differential immune contributions. Model simulations show rapid bacterial replication post-inoculation (growth rates: BTG=1.47, BG=1.18, BT=1.01, B=0.06), with neutrophils responding fastest, followed by IgA and IgG. The relative contribution of these immune components to bacterial neutralization varied by infection type, with neutrophils dominating in B-only infections while combinations of neutrophils with IgG or IgA were important in co-infected groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C39-C52, C69, C70, and C73 describe model results fitted to experimental data using Bayesian methods (HMC in Stan). The model successfully captured empirical trends (C40) with parameter estimates provided in Table 2. Model validation and selection procedures (Appendix 4-5) support the approach. However, the model represents a simplified immune response and makes explicit assumptions about additive effects.

results.result: The model framework could not explain rapid within-host variation in shedding intensity observed between consecutive samplings. Rabbits showed rapid fluctuations where bursts of bacteria alternated with low or no shedding within days. The authors suggest that fast, local changes at the respiratory tissue level (e.g., tissue inflammation, mucosa-level bacterial control, mucus discharge) likely played a more important role than systemic immune dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C58-C60, C93, and C98 acknowledge a clear limitation of the modeling approach. The authors transparently report that their model scale could not capture rapid individual-level variation (C59, C98) and provide speculative but reasonable explanations for this limitation (C6, C60, C93). This represents an honest assessment of model capabilities versus observations.

results.result: Model simulations reveal distinct temporal shedding patterns among co-infection types. Peak shedding occurred at 9-12 days post-infection for co-infected groups, with BTG showing the most rapid increase, highest peak (14,185 CFU/day), and slowest decline, suggesting possible synergistic effects of the two helminths. BT showed the fastest decline, while BG was intermediate. Early shedding decline (first 90 days) was attributed to immune-mediated bacterial clearance from lungs, while later reduced shedding reflected weak control in the nasal cavity.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 and C71-C77 present model-derived interpretations of shedding dynamics. While the temporal patterns are based on model fits to data, several claims are speculative (C56, C75, C76, C77 use language like 'suggesting,' 'could have been,' 'probably'). The mechanistic explanations for differences between helminth species (C75, C76) and synergistic effects (C56, C77) are plausible inferences but lack direct experimental validation. The model for B-only rabbits also has acknowledged limitations due to missing early data.

results.result: Sensitivity analysis reveals that bacterial neutralization rate and immune growth rate are key determinants of shedding dynamics. Increases in neutralization rate (μc) and immune growth rate (μa) led to proportional decreases in peak shedding and time to peak. Among immune variables, neutrophil and IgG rates had the strongest negative impact on shedding. Bacterial growth rate (r) positively correlated with peak shedding. Co-infected groups were more sensitive to immune parameter changes than B-only rabbits.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C66 describe sensitivity analysis results (Appendix 2) that systematically varied model parameters to assess their impact on shedding. This is a standard modeling approach that provides insight into which parameters most influence outcomes. The findings are internally consistent with the model structure and help interpret the biological mechanisms.

results.result: B. bronchiseptica shedding exhibits large variation at three levels: between infection types, between hosts within each type, and within individual hosts over time. High shedders were concentrated in the first 60 days post-infection. Up to 55% of shedding events were null (no shedding despite infection), with the highest percentage in B-only rabbits (56.2%) and lowest in BTG (25.8%). The BTG group showed the largest variation in shedding levels (Negative Binomial k=0.21).
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C30 and C97 describe direct experimental observations with appropriate statistical characterization (Negative Binomial fitting). The multi-level variation is well-documented in Figures 1-3. Sample sizes are adequate (13-24 rabbits per group after excluding non-shedders), and the descriptive statistics are appropriate for the data type.

results.result: The authors infer that helminth co-infection should increase the probability of B. bronchiseptica onward transmission and that the risk likely increases non-linearly given the magnitude and frequency of supershedding. They conclude that understanding helminth modulation of respiratory infections is important for developing targeted treatments and that detecting/controlling supershedders is critical for reducing disease outbreak risk.
results.evaluation: Claims C33, C101, C104, and C105 represent inferences and implications rather than direct experimental findings. While the increased shedding in co-infected hosts (established in other results) logically suggests higher transmission probability, actual transmission was not measured in these experiments. The claims about non-linear transmission risk (C101) and public health implications (C104, C105) are reasonable extrapolations but speculative without transmission studies or epidemiological data.

results.result: Both T. retortaeformis and G. strigosum elicit Th-2 immune responses and are commonly found in rabbit populations. Field studies show B. bronchiseptica prevalence of 88-97% in free-living rabbits, with 65% co-infected with B. bronchiseptica and G. strigosum, and approximately 60% of adult rabbits carrying BTG triple infections.
results.evaluation: Claims C74 and C78-C81 cite previous published work (C74, C79, C80) and unpublished field data (C81). The Th-2 response claim is well-supported by multiple citations. The field prevalence data provide ecological context for the experimental findings, though C81 relies on unpublished data which limits independent verification.

results.result: Previous studies support the role of neutrophils and antibodies in B. bronchiseptica control. Boolean modeling indicated antigen-antibody complexes and phagocytosis are important for lung clearance. Mouse studies showed serum antibodies clear bacteria from lungs/trachea within 3 days, and IgA is necessary for nasal cavity reduction. Evidence from other co-infection systems (P. aeruginosa-H. polygyrus in mice) shows gut helminths can enhance respiratory neutrophil responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C90 summarize prior published work with appropriate citations. These claims establish the scientific foundation for the current study's focus on neutrophils, IgA, and IgG. The citations appear relevant and support the mechanistic framework used in the modeling approach.

results.result: The authors propose that Th2 immune interference from T. retortaeformis and G. strigosum contributed to increased B. bronchiseptica shedding levels and duration, though this anti-inflammatory response was not strong enough to prevent bacterial clearance from the lower respiratory tract.
results.evaluation: Claims C91 and C92 represent a proposed mechanism integrating the findings. While the Th1/Th2 paradigm is well-established and helminth-induced Th2 responses are documented (C19, C74), the specific contribution of Th2 interference to the observed shedding patterns is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. The study did not measure Th1/Th2 cytokines or directly test this mechanism, making this an uncertain but plausible interpretation.

results.result: Fast, intermittent shedding has been reported in other pathogen systems (both single and co-infections), including Epstein-Barr virus in healthy carriers where variation in shedding level and frequency occurs at the individual level over time.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 cite relevant comparative literature showing that rapid shedding variation is not unique to this system. The citations support the generalizability of the within-host temporal variation observed and provide context for the modeling limitations.

results.result: The experimental design used New Zealand White male rabbits infected with B. bronchiseptica strain RB50 and/or helminth larvae at doses following natural infections. Infections were followed for 120-150 days with serial sacrifices. Shedding was assessed by direct contact with agar plates, and immune responses (neutrophils, IgA, IgG) were measured from blood samples using standard laboratory methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C119 describe methodological details that are clearly stated and follow standard microbiological and immunological protocols. The experimental design is appropriate for the research questions, with adequate sample sizes (16-32 infected rabbits per group) and controls. Methods are sufficiently detailed for reproducibility.

results.result: The mathematical model assumes bacterial neutralization occurs through additive effects of neutrophils, IgA, and IgG, and that helminths affect infection by altering the magnitude and time course of these immune responses. Model fitting used Hamiltonian Monte Carlo in Stan 2.18.0. The full model (all three immune variables) was statistically superior to reduced models based on BIC.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C124 describe modeling assumptions and methods. The assumptions are explicitly stated and represent reasonable simplifications. The use of Bayesian HMC is appropriate for this type of hierarchical model. Model selection using BIC (C124, Appendix 5) provides statistical justification for including all three immune variables. However, the additive assumption (C121) is a simplification that may not capture more complex immune interactions.

results.result: Background claims establish that co-infected hosts may facilitate transmission and supershedding; that B. bronchiseptica is a contagious respiratory bacterium cleared from lower airways via Th1 responses involving neutrophils and antibodies but persisting in nasal cavity; that helminths stimulate Th2 responses interfering with Th1; and that helminth infections are globally prevalent with respiratory infections being a major cause of death.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C22, C67, C102-C103 provide background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These claims set the scientific context and rationale for the study. The citations appear relevant and the background claims are consistent with established knowledge in infectious disease ecology and immunology.

results.result: B. bronchiseptica is removed from lungs and trachea but persists in the nasal cavity, a pattern observed in both the current experiments and previous mouse studies.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 is supported by citations to previous experimental work including the authors' own studies. This anatomical pattern of clearance is important for interpreting the shedding dynamics and is consistent across multiple studies and species.

results.result: IgG reached asymptotic values around 20 days post-infection and remained high throughout trials, while IgA peaked around day 20 and slowly decreased thereafter without returning to baseline.
results.evaluation: Claim C44 describes temporal antibody dynamics directly observed in the experimental data and shown in Figures 5 and 6. The patterns are clearly visible in the figures and consistent with typical antibody response kinetics.

results.result: Co-infected rabbits sniffled more frequently than B. bronchiseptica-only animals based on personal observation during experiments.
results.evaluation: Claim C61 is based on anecdotal observation (Pathak's personal observation) without systematic quantification. While this observation may be accurate and could contribute to shedding variation, it lacks the rigor of systematic measurement and statistical analysis. This represents an interesting observation that would benefit from formal quantification in future work.
